claim: Selective transcription of individual protein coding genes does not occur in trypanosomes.
source: Selective transcription of individual protein coding genes does not occur in trypanosomes and the cellular copy number of each mRNA must be determined post-transcriptionally.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that is supported by the extensive background literature cited in the introduction.

claim: The cellular copy number of each mRNA in trypanosomes must be determined post-transcriptionally.
source: Selective transcription of individual protein coding genes does not occur in trypanosomes and the cellular copy number of each mRNA must be determined post-transcriptionally.
evidence: This follows logically from the lack of selective transcription and is supported by the literature on trypanosome gene expression.

claim: A novel codon usage metric, the gene expression codon adaptation index (geCAI), was developed that maximised the relationship between codon choice and the measured abundance for a transcriptome.
source: First, a novel codon usage metric, the gene expression codon adaptation index (geCAI), was developed that maximised the relationship between codon choice and the measured abundance for a transcriptome.
evidence: The development of geCAI is described in detail in the Results section with methodology and data.

claim: geCAI predictions of mRNA levels were successful over a 25-fold range, similar to the variation in endogenous mRNAs.
source: Second, geCAI predictions of mRNA levels were tested using differently coded GFP transgenes and were successful over a 25-fold range, similar to the variation in endogenous mRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using GFP transgenes shown in Figure 4.

claim: Translation was necessary for the accelerated mRNA turnover resulting from codon choice.
source: Third, translation was necessary for the accelerated mRNA turnover resulting from codon choice.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments using hairpin structures in the 5'UTR to block translation, shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: In trypanosomes, the information determining the levels of most mRNAs resides in the open reading frame.
source: Thus, in trypanosomes, the information determining the levels of most mRNAs resides in the open reading frame and translation is required to access this information.
evidence: This is supported by the geCAI analysis and GFP experiments showing that codon choice in the ORF determines mRNA levels.

claim: Translation is required to access the information in the ORF that determines mRNA levels.
source: Thus, in trypanosomes, the information determining the levels of most mRNAs resides in the open reading frame and translation is required to access this information.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing that blocking translation prevents codon-mediated mRNA turnover.

claim: RNA polymerase II dependent transcription of protein coding genes is polycistronic in trypanosomatids.
source: In trypanosomatids, RNA polymerase II dependent transcription of protein coding genes is polycistronic (Van der Ploeg, 1986; Worthey et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Van der Ploeg, 1986 and Worthey et al., 2003.

claim: Individual monocistronic mRNAs in trypanosomatids are produced after co-transcriptional processing by trans-splicing a 39 nucleotide, capped, exon to the 5' end and linked endonucleolytic cleavage and polyadenylation of the upstream mRNA.
source: Individual monocistronic mRNAs are produced after co-transcriptional processing by trans-splicing a 39 nucleotide, capped, exon to the 5' end and linked endonucleolytic cleavage and polyadenylation of the upstream mRNA (Sutton and Boothroyd, 1986; Murphy et al., 1986; Ullu et al., 1993; Matthews et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing the trans-splicing mechanism.

claim: Protein coding genes in trypanosomatids occur in tandemly arrayed clusters containing up to hundreds of genes in one transcription unit.
source: This mechanism of mRNA transcription has co-evolved with the structure of the genome; protein coding genes occur in tandemly arrayed clusters containing up to hundreds of genes in one transcription unit (Ivens et al., 2005; Berriman et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genome sequencing studies.

claim: Transcription start sites for gene clusters in trypanosomatids have been identified.
source: The transcription start sites for these gene clusters have been identified (Kolev et al., 2010) and are marked by histone variants (Siegel et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kolev et al., 2010 and Siegel et al., 2009.

claim: Transcription start sites in trypanosomatids are marked by histone variants.
source: The transcription start sites for these gene clusters have been identified (Kolev et al., 2010) and are marked by histone variants (Siegel et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Siegel et al., 2009.

claim: A GT-rich promoter element has been identified in trypanosomatids that can both initiate transcription and cause histone variant deposition.
source: and although the nature of promoters remains incompletely defined, a GT-rich promoter element has been identified that can both initiate transcription and cause histone variant deposition (Wedel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wedel et al., 2017.

claim: There is remarkable synteny between the genomes of trypanosomatid species that diverged hundreds of millions of years ago.
source: There is remarkable synteny between the genomes of trypanosomatid species that diverged hundreds of millions of years ago (El-Sayed et al., 2005) suggesting a functional organisation of genes within polycistronic transcription units.
evidence: This is supported by citation to El-Sayed et al., 2005.

claim: Genes up-regulated during heat shock in trypanosomatids tend to be distal to the transcription start site.
source: For example, genes up-regulated during heat shock tend to be distal to the transcription start site so that they continue to be transcribed by elongating RNA polymerase II for >60 min after transcription initiation has stopped as a consequence of the stress (Kelly et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kelly et al., 2012.

claim: There is no convincing evidence for selective regulation of RNA polymerase II transcription of individual genes or transcription units in trypanosomatids.
source: As yet, there is no convincing evidence for selective regulation of RNA polymerase II transcription of individual genes or transcription units.
evidence: This is a statement based on the absence of evidence in the literature.

claim: The disparate levels of individual mRNAs within a trypanosome cell is dependent solely on post-transcriptional processes.
source: In the absence of regulation based on selective transcription of individual genes, the disparate levels of individual mRNAs within a trypanosome cell is dependent solely on post-transcriptional processes.
evidence: This is an inference from the lack of selective transcription.

claim: α- and β-tubulins in trypanosomatids are encoded by a tandem array of 19 copies of each gene.
source: For example, α- and β-tubulins are encoded by a tandem array of 19 copies of each gene (Ersfeld et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ersfeld et al., 1998.

claim: The majority of genes in trypanosomatids are single copy and are expressed in the cell at different levels.
source: However, the majority of genes are single copy and are expressed in the cell at different levels (Kolev et al., 2010) so mechanisms for regulation of mRNA abundance must exist and these must act post-transcriptionally.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kolev et al., 2010 and inference about post-transcriptional regulation.

claim: The abundance of each mRNA in trypanosomatids is probably regulated at several levels during its production/degradation cycle.
source: It is probable that the abundance of each mRNA is regulated at several levels during its production/degradation cycle: the rate of maturation against the decay rate of the pre-mRNA in the nucleus; the rate of export to the cytoplasm against the half-life of the mature mRNA in the nucleus; the half-life of the mature mRNA in the cytoplasm (Haanstra et al., 2008).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to Haanstra et al., 2008.

claim: Cis-elements have been identified in the 3'UTRs of trypanosomatid mRNAs that differentially affect stability and/or rate of translation in specific developmental stages.
source: Cis-elements have been identified in the 3'UTRs that differentially affect stability and/or rate of translation of mRNAs in specific developmental stages; the best characterised being those in procyclin mRNAs (Furger et al., 1997; Hehl et al., 1994), cytochrome oxidase subunits (Mayho et al., 2006), and a short stem loop, necessary and sufficient for response to external purine concentration (Fernández-Moya et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies identifying these elements.

claim: Manipulation of cis-elements in trypanosomatid mRNAs rarely quantitatively recapitulates the observed variations in mRNA levels in vivo.
source: Manipulation of these elements rarely quantitatively recapitulates the observed variations in mRNA levels in vivo whereas transfer of an entire 3'UTR can (Webb et al., 2005a), this may reflect a combinatorial mechanism necessary for complete developmental regulation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Webb et al., 2005a and inference about combinatorial mechanisms.

claim: Transfer of an entire 3'UTR in trypanosomatids can quantitatively recapitulate observed variations in mRNA levels in vivo.
source: Manipulation of these elements rarely quantitatively recapitulates the observed variations in mRNA levels in vivo whereas transfer of an entire 3'UTR can (Webb et al., 2005a), this may reflect a combinatorial mechanism necessary for complete developmental regulation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Webb et al., 2005a.

claim: Over expression of RBP6 in trypanosomatids is sufficient to drive PCFs through several successive developmental transitions.
source: The most spectacular examples of these include the RNA recognition motif-containing proteins RPB6 and RPB10. Over expression of RBP6 is sufficient to drive PCFs through several successive developmental transitions (Kolev et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kolev et al., 2012.

claim: Over expression of RBP10 in trypanosomatids causes a PCF transcriptome to switch to BSF.
source: and over expression of RBP10 causes a PCF transcriptome to switch to BSF (Mugo and Clayton, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mugo and Clayton, 2017.

claim: RBP42 binds within the open reading frame of many mRNAs that encode proteins involved in energy metabolism in trypanosomatids.
source: Other RNA binding proteins have been shown to have specific effects on sets of mRNAs, for example RBP42 binds within the open reading frame (ORF) of many mRNAs that encode proteins involved in energy metabolism (Das et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Das et al., 2012.

claim: ZPF3 binds the LII cis-element in the EP1 procyclin mRNA 3' UTR and displaces a negative regulator of translation leading to increased EP1 protein abundance.
source: Similarly, ZPF3 binds the LII cis-element in the EP1 procyclin mRNA 3' UTR and displaces a negative regulator of translation leading to increased EP1 protein abundance (Walrad et al., 2009; Walrad et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Walrad et al., 2009 and Walrad et al., 2012.

claim: There is a codon bias in highly expressed genes in T. brucei and related trypanosomatid species.
source: However, the model is derived from a consideration of a small subset of mRNAs prone to dramatic regulation and further, it fails to consider work that demonstrated a codon bias in highly expressed genes in T. brucei and related trypanosomatid species (Horn, 2008; Seward and Kelly, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Horn, 2008 and Seward and Kelly, 2016.

claim: The use of favoured codons in highly expressed genes in trypanosomatids correlated with cognate tRNA gene numbers.
source: The use of favoured codons in highly expressed genes correlated with cognate tRNA gene numbers and led to the suggestion that translational selection was likely to act on highly abundant genes.
evidence: This is an observation from previous studies that led to a hypothesis about translational selection.

claim: Selection in trypanosomatids was acting in proportion to mRNA abundance to reduce the biosynthesis requirements of those transcripts.
source: Moreover, selection was also acting in proportion to mRNA abundance to reduce the biosynthesis requirements of those transcripts (Seward and Kelly, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Seward and Kelly, 2016.

claim: Codon choice is a major determinant of mRNA levels in yeast.
source: More recently, it has been shown that codon choice is a major determinant of mRNA levels in yeast (Presnyak et al., 2015) operating through a system that monitors the rate of translation elongation involving displacement of the RNA helicase DHH1 which in turn affects the activity of the NOT1 deadenylase complex (Radhakrishnan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Presnyak et al., 2015 and Radhakrishnan et al., 2016.

claim: Codon choice in yeast operates through a system that monitors the rate of translation elongation involving displacement of the RNA helicase DHH1 which in turn affects the activity of the NOT1 deadenylase complex.
source: More recently, it has been shown that codon choice is a major determinant of mRNA levels in yeast (Presnyak et al., 2015) operating through a system that monitors the rate of translation elongation involving displacement of the RNA helicase DHH1 which in turn affects the activity of the NOT1 deadenylase complex (Radhakrishnan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Radhakrishnan et al., 2016.

claim: Codon choice is an important determinant of maternal mRNA turnover in zebra fish.
source: Further, codon choice is also an important determinant of maternal mRNA turnover in zebra fish (Mishima et al., 2016) and Drosophila (Bazzini et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mishima et al., 2016.

claim: Codon choice is an important determinant of maternal mRNA turnover in Drosophila.
source: Further, codon choice is also an important determinant of maternal mRNA turnover in zebra fish (Mishima et al., 2016) and Drosophila (Bazzini et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bazzini et al., 2016.

claim: Adjusting the open reading frame to codons that were under-represented in highly expressed mRNAs was more effective at reducing transgene expression than other modifications including mutating the AG acceptor dinucleotide to AA in the trans-splicing site, using a synthetic 5'UTR, and using a 3'UTR from a low abundance mRNA.
source: Of the approaches used, adjusting the open reading frame (ORF) to codons that were under-represented in highly expressed mRNAs was more effective than other modifications including mutating the AG acceptor dinucleotide to AA in the trans-splicing site (Siegel et al., 2005), using a synthetic 5'UTR (Siegel et al., 2005) and using a 3'UTR from a low abundance mRNA (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: There was a correlation between levels of MS2bp-GFP-nls mRNA and protein levels, including the codon altered transgene mRNA.
source: The relative levels of the MS2bp-GFP-nls mRNA were then estimated by northern blotting (Figure 1), this showed a correlation between levels of MS2bp-GFP-nls mRNA and protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) levels, including the codon altered transgene mRNA.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Different GFP ORFs produced a range of fluorescence levels when integrated into the tubulin locus of procyclic form trypanosomes.
source: On analysing transgenic cell lines, it was immediately apparent that different GFP ORFs produced a range of fluorescence levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Pearson's correlation coefficient between the measurement of GFP by flow cytometry and estimates of GFP expression from western blotting was R2 = 0.965.
source: The Pearson's correlation coefficient between the measurement of GFP by flow cytometry and estimates of GFP expression from western blotting was R2 = 0.965; validating the use of GFP fluorescence as a measure of total GFP protein.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: GFP fluorescence is a valid measure of total GFP protein in trypanosomes.
source: The Pearson's correlation coefficient between the measurement of GFP by flow cytometry and estimates of GFP expression from western blotting was R2 = 0.965; validating the use of GFP fluorescence as a measure of total GFP protein.
evidence: This is an inference from the high correlation between fluorescence and western blot measurements.

claim: The geCAI calculation used measured expression levels of mRNAs from 5136 single copy genes.
source: To calculate the codon values, the measured expression levels of mRNAs from 5136 single copy genes were used.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology used to develop geCAI.

claim: mRNAs with >2 fold differential expression when BSF and PCF trypanosomes were compared were excluded from the geCAI calculation.
source: This set of genes represented the genome with the following exclusions: (i) mRNAs with >2 fold differential expression when BSF and PCF trypanosomes were compared (Kelly et al., 2017) as the mRNA abundance are likely to be modulated by cis-acting RNA binding proteins and thus obscure the codon score learning process.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology used to develop geCAI.

claim: mRNAs encoded by single copy genes without a homologue in at least one other kinetoplastid species were excluded from the geCAI calculation.
source: (ii) mRNAs encoded by single copy genes without a homologue in at least one other kinetoplastid species, this was a mechanism to exclude any potentially spurious ORFs that may not encode proteins.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology used to develop geCAI.

claim: mRNAs encoded by multicopy genes families were excluded from the geCAI calculation.
source: (iii) mRNAs encoded by multicopy genes families as the accuracy of TPM calculations is compromised by uncertainty of copy number and associated errors in allocation of many sequence reads to individual genes.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology used to develop geCAI.

claim: The Spearman's rank correlation coefficient between geCAI scores for the 5136 ORFs and mRNA abundances was ρ = 0.55.
source: When mRNA abundance expressed as TPM was plotted against the ORF geCAI scores (Supplementary file 4), the Spearman's rank correlation coefficient for the 5136 mRNAs was ρ = 0.55 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A mid-log phase PCF cell contains approximately 50000 mRNA molecules.
source: A mid-log phase PCF cell contains approximately 50000 mRNA molecules (Dhalia et al., 2006) and so 20 TPM is equivalent to one mRNA molecule/cell
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dhalia et al., 2006.

claim: 20 TPM is equivalent to one mRNA molecule per cell in procyclic form trypanosomes.
source: A mid-log phase PCF cell contains approximately 50000 mRNA molecules (Dhalia et al., 2006) and so 20 TPM is equivalent to one mRNA molecule/cell
evidence: This is a calculation based on the total number of mRNA molecules per cell.

claim: The range of transcript abundance for the vast majority of single copy genes in trypanosomes is between ~1 and 40 mRNAs per diploid gene pair per cell.
source: so the range of transcript abundance for the vast majority is between ~1 and 40 mRNAs/diploid gene pair/cell.
evidence: This is derived from the TPM measurements and the calculation of mRNA molecules per cell.

claim: CAI and tAI provided limited correlation with measured mRNA levels in trypanosomes with Spearman's rank correlation coefficients of ρ = 0.16 and ρ = 0.13 respectively.
source: Of the tested methods, CAI (Carbone et al., 2005) and tAI (Tuller et al., 2010) provided the best correlation but the predictive capacity was limited with Spearman's rank correlation coefficients of ρ = 0.16 and ρ = 0.13 respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: CAI and tAI assume the effectiveness of the 'best' codon for each amino acid is equivalent.
source: These measures may be unsuitable for this type of analysis as each assumes the effectiveness of the 'best' codon for each amino acid is equivalent, for example that the most efficient codon for glycine will have the same effect as the most efficient codon for alanine.
evidence: This is a statement about the assumptions underlying CAI and tAI metrics.

claim: There is evidence that the most efficient codon for one amino acid does not have the same effect as the most efficient codon for another amino acid.
source: There is evidence that this is not the case (Gardin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gardin et al., 2014.

claim: The geCAI score was able to predict GFP protein abundance with 84% accuracy (Pearson's correlation coefficient, r2 = 0.84).
source: The GFP protein abundance was expressed relative to eGFP and plotted against geCAI score (Figure 4A); the geCAI score was able to predict GFP protein abundance with 84% accuracy (Pearson's correlation coefficient, r2 = 0.84).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The correlation coefficient between GFP protein abundance and CAI was r2 = 0.25.
source: This compared favourably with the correlation coefficients between GFP protein abundance and either CAI (r2 = 0.25) or tAI (r2 = 0.61) (Supplementary file 6B).
evidence: This is supported by data in Supplementary file 6B.

claim: The correlation coefficient between GFP protein abundance and tAI was r2 = 0.61.
source: This compared favourably with the correlation coefficients between GFP protein abundance and either CAI (r2 = 0.25) or tAI (r2 = 0.61) (Supplementary file 6B).
evidence: This is supported by data in Supplementary file 6B.

claim: The Pearson's correlation coefficient between GFP mRNA levels and geCAI was r2 = 0.92.
source: The Pearson's correlation coefficient between GFP mRNA levels and geCAI was r2 = 0.92 (Figure 4B and Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and Supplementary file 7.

claim: Codon use was the major determinant of steady state levels for the transgene derived GFP mRNA and protein.
source: Therefore, as the genomic integration site, UTRs and amino acid sequence were all identical, codon use was the major determinant of steady state levels for the transgene derived GFP mRNA and protein.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental design where only codon usage varied between constructs.

claim: The ~25 fold range of GFP mRNA levels is similar to the range present in mRNAs from single copy genes in the transcriptome.
source: The ~25 fold range of GFP mRNA levels, 2.5 to 60 mRNAs/diploid gene pair equivalent/cell (Figure 4B) is similar to the range present in mRNAs from single copy genes in the transcriptome.
evidence: This is a comparison between the experimental GFP data and the endogenous transcriptome data.

claim: Altering codon use can account for the range of steady state level of most mRNAs in trypanosomes.
source: Thus, altering codon use can account for the range of steady state level of most mRNAs and the geCAI score is a good predictor of mRNA level for single copy genes not subject to developmental regulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the GFP experiments and transcriptome analysis.

claim: The geCAI score is a good predictor of mRNA level for single copy genes not subject to developmental regulation in trypanosomes.
source: Thus, altering codon use can account for the range of steady state level of most mRNAs and the geCAI score is a good predictor of mRNA level for single copy genes not subject to developmental regulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the GFP experiments and transcriptome analysis.

claim: Discrepancy between geCAI score for a gene and the observed mRNA or protein abundance for that gene is an indicator that other regulatory mechanisms, such as cis-acting RNA binding proteins may be acting on that gene to modulate mRNA abundance.
source: Furthermore, discrepancy between geCAI score for a gene and the observed mRNA or protein abundance for that gene is an indicator that other regulatory mechanisms, such as cis-acting RNA binding proteins may be acting on that gene to modulate mRNA abundance.
evidence: This is an inference about how to interpret deviations from geCAI predictions.

claim: mRNAs for cytosolic ribosomal proteins have significantly higher geCAI scores than those encoding mitochondrial ribosomal proteins.
source: The more abundant cytosolic ribosomal protein mRNAs had higher geCAI scores than the less abundant mitochondrial ribosome protein mRNAs (Figure 5 and Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5 and Supplementary file 8.

claim: The mean geCAI scores (±SD) were 0.439 (±0.034) for cytoplasmic and 0.378 (±0.033) for mitochondrial ribosomal protein mRNAs.
source: The mean geCAI scores (±SD) were 0.439 (±0.034) for cytoplasmic and 0.378 (±0.033) for mitochondrial ribosomal protein mRNAs respectively.
evidence: This is a statistical summary of the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The probability of the difference in geCAI scores between cytoplasmic and mitochondrial ribosomal protein mRNAs arising by chance is <0.00001.
source: The probability of this difference arising by chance is <0.00001 (unpaired two-sample t test with equal variance).
evidence: This is a statistical test of the significance of the difference in geCAI scores.

claim: More abundant proteins in trypanosomes are encoded by mRNAs with higher geCAI scores.
source: These measurements are consistent with more abundant proteins are encoded by mRNAs with higher geCAI scores.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of cytoplasmic and mitochondrial ribosomal protein mRNAs.

claim: The two GFPs with the highest geCAI scores (eGFP: 0.547 and GFP P3: 0.520) had no detectable decay over the time course of 60 min after inhibition of trans-splicing with sinefungin.
source: The two GFPs with the highest geCAI scores (eGFP: 0.547 and GFP P3: 0.520) had no detectable decay over the time course of 60 min, these both have geCAI scores greater than nearly all endogenous mRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Three GFP mRNAs with lower geCAI scores (GFP P2: 0.493, GFP 226: 0.432 and GFP 102: 0.375) had a rate of decay inversely proportional to the geCAI value.
source: The three other GFPs with lower geCAI scores (GFP P2: 0.493, GFP 226: 0.432 and GFP 102: 0.375) had a rate of decay inversely proportional to the geCAI value (Figure 6B and Supplementary file 9).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6B and Supplementary file 9.

claim: For three GFP mRNAs with lower geCAI scores, decay to 50% occurred between 10 and ~80 min, similar to the range of half-lives reported for endogenous mRNAs.
source: For these three GFP mRNAs decay to 50% occurred between 10 and ~80 min, similar to the range of half-lives reported for endogenous mRNAs (Fadda et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison with published data on endogenous mRNA half-lives.

claim: The Spearman's rank correlation coefficient between mRNA half-lives from Fadda et al., 2014 and geCAI scores from the cognate transcriptome was ρ = 0.22.
source: The Spearman's rank correlation coefficient was ρ = 0.22 for the cognate geCAI values and ρ = 0.33 for the geCAI values used in this study.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Spearman's rank correlation coefficient between mRNA half-lives from Fadda et al., 2014 and geCAI scores from this study was ρ = 0.33.
source: The Spearman's rank correlation coefficient was ρ = 0.22 for the cognate geCAI values and ρ = 0.33 for the geCAI values used in this study.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: geCAI scores can explain a significant proportion of variance in mRNA turnover rates at a transcriptome wide level.
source: Thus, geCAI scores calculated using either study can explain a significant proportion of variance in mRNA turnover rates at a transcriptome wide level.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation between geCAI scores and mRNA half-lives.

claim: There was no detectable expression of GFP by flow cytometry in any of the cell lines containing a transgene with a 48 base hairpin in the 5'UTR.
source: As expected, there was no detectable expression of GFP by flow cytometry in any of the cell lines containing a transgene with a hairpin (Supplementary file 6C and 6D), therefore the hairpin-containing mRNAs were not translated.
evidence: This is supported by data in Supplementary file 6C and 6D.

claim: The hairpin-containing GFP mRNAs were not translated.
source: As expected, there was no detectable expression of GFP by flow cytometry in any of the cell lines containing a transgene with a hairpin (Supplementary file 6C and 6D), therefore the hairpin-containing mRNAs were not translated.
evidence: This is an inference from the lack of GFP protein expression.

claim: The effect of inclusion of the hairpin in the 5'UTR was to stabilise the GFP mRNAs.
source: Measurements of the mRNA levels by quantitative northern blotting revealed that the effect of inclusion of the hairpin in the 5'UTR was to stabilise the GFP mRNAs (Figure 7A and Supplementary file 6E)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7A and Supplementary file 6E.

claim: The lower the geCAI score, the greater the relative increase in abundance of the hairpin to control mRNAs, from 1.4-fold for eGFP (geCAI = 0.547) to 14-fold for GFP 102 (geCAI = 0.375).
source: and the lower the geCAI score the greater the relative increase in abundance of the hairpin to control mRNAs from 1.4-fold for eGFP (geCAI = 0.547) to 14-fold for GFP 102 (geCAI = 0.375) (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Translation of an ORF is necessary for the variation in mRNA half-life conferred by the geCAI.
source: These observations provide evidence that: (i) the translation of an ORF is necessary for the variation in mRNA half-life conferred by the geCAI,
evidence: This is an inference from the hairpin experiments showing that blocking translation stabilizes mRNAs.

claim: The different GFP mRNA levels result from active destabilisation.
source: (ii) the different GFP mRNA levels result from active destabilisation,
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that blocking translation increases mRNA levels.

claim: None of the mRNAs with differently coded GFPs are inherently unstable due to sequence alone.
source: and (iii) none of the mRNAs with differently coded GFPs are inherently unstable due to sequence alone.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that all GFP mRNAs are stabilized when translation is blocked.

claim: A 12 bp stem loop in the 5'UTR resulted in eGFP protein expression that was 11% of that from the parental transgene without a hairpin in the 5'UTR.
source: In contrast, a 12 bp stem loop resulted in eGFP protein expression that was 11% of that from the parental transgene without a hairpin in the 5'UTR (Supplementary file 6F).
evidence: This is supported by data in Supplementary file 6F.

claim: The presence of the 12 bp stem loop resulted in a modest reduction to 76% in the steady state GFP mRNA levels.
source: the presence of the 12 bp stem loop resulted in a modest reduction to 76% in the steady state GFP mRNA levels (p=0.13 for a difference between the mRNAs with and without a 12 bp stem loop; unpaired two-sample t test).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8 and Supplementary file 6G.

claim: A nine-fold reduction in the frequency of translation has only a small effect on the GFP mRNA levels.
source: This observation that a nine-fold reduction in the frequency of translation has only a small effect on the GFP mRNA levels favours a model in which geCAI score is interpreted by the translating ribosome by a mechanism mostly independent of ribosome density/frequency of translation, possibly the rate of ribosome progression.
evidence: This is an inference from the 12 bp stem loop experiment.

claim: geCAI score is interpreted by the translating ribosome by a mechanism mostly independent of ribosome density/frequency of translation, possibly the rate of ribosome progression.
source: This observation that a nine-fold reduction in the frequency of translation has only a small effect on the GFP mRNA levels favours a model in which geCAI score is interpreted by the translating ribosome by a mechanism mostly independent of ribosome density/frequency of translation, possibly the rate of ribosome progression.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that reduced translation frequency has little effect on mRNA levels.

claim: There is a correlation between ribosome density and mRNA levels in trypanosomes.
source: There is a correlation between ribosome density and mRNA levels but there is also great variation in the ribosome density on different mRNAs with similar expression levels (Jensen et al., 2014) indicating frequency of translation/ribosome density alone is not sufficient to determine translationally regulated mRNA turnover.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jensen et al., 2014.

claim: There is great variation in the ribosome density on different mRNAs with similar expression levels in trypanosomes.
source: There is a correlation between ribosome density and mRNA levels but there is also great variation in the ribosome density on different mRNAs with similar expression levels (Jensen et al., 2014) indicating frequency of translation/ribosome density alone is not sufficient to determine translationally regulated mRNA turnover.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jensen et al., 2014.

claim: Frequency of translation/ribosome density alone is not sufficient to determine translationally regulated mRNA turnover in trypanosomes.
source: There is a correlation between ribosome density and mRNA levels but there is also great variation in the ribosome density on different mRNAs with similar expression levels (Jensen et al., 2014) indicating frequency of translation/ribosome density alone is not sufficient to determine translationally regulated mRNA turnover.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of variation in ribosome density at similar expression levels.

claim: The Pearson's correlation coefficient between ribosome footprint levels and geCAI was R2 = 0.141 and 0.244 for two sets of ribosome density values.
source: The Pearson's correlation coefficient between ribosome footprint levels and geCAI was R2 = 0.141 and 0.244 for the two sets of ribosome density values.
evidence: This is supported by data in Supplementary file 10.

claim: Occupancy/frequency of translation can explain a significant component of the geCAI measure.
source: Thus occupancy/frequency of translation can explain a significant component of the geCAI measure, but suggests a model in which geCAI mediated mRNA turnover is also dependent on other factors.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation between ribosome density and geCAI.

claim: geCAI mediated mRNA turnover is dependent on factors other than occupancy/frequency of translation.
source: Thus occupancy/frequency of translation can explain a significant component of the geCAI measure, but suggests a model in which geCAI mediated mRNA turnover is also dependent on other factors.
evidence: This is speculation based on the incomplete correlation between ribosome density and geCAI.

claim: mRNAs upregulated in PCFs are largely expressed at higher levels than would be predicted by geCAI alone.

source: In contrast, mRNAs downregulated in PCFs (upregulated in BSFs) are expressed at levels lower than predicted by geCAI.

claim: Developmental regulation in trypanosomes results from both stabilisation and destabilisation pathways that act in concert to modulate the geCAI determined mRNA levels.
source: Taken together, these measurements provide evidence that developmental regulation results from both stabilisation and destabilisation pathways that act in concert to modulate the geCAI determined mRNA levels.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that developmentally regulated mRNAs deviate from geCAI predictions in both directions.

claim: Trypanosomatids have evolved separately from other eukaryotic lineages for ~500 million years.
source: Trypanosomatids have evolved separately from other eukaryotic lineages for ~500 million years (Lukeš et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lukeš et al., 2014.

claim: The core gene expression machinery present in the last eukaryotic common ancestor has been largely conserved in trypanosomatids.
source: Over this time the core gene expression machinery present in the last eukaryotic common ancestor has been largely conserved but selective transcription of individual genes by RNA polymerase II has been lost and individual mRNAs arise by co-transcriptional processing of polycistronically transcribed precursors.
evidence: This is a statement based on comparative genomics and established knowledge.

claim: Selective transcription of individual genes by RNA polymerase II has been lost in trypanosomatids.
source: Over this time the core gene expression machinery present in the last eukaryotic common ancestor has been largely conserved but selective transcription of individual genes by RNA polymerase II has been lost and individual mRNAs arise by co-transcriptional processing of polycistronically transcribed precursors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about trypanosome gene expression.

claim: Codon use is central to the regulation of mRNA levels in trypanosomes.
source: The major finding presented here is that codon use is central to the regulation of mRNA levels in trypanosomes.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data.

claim: The geCAI score for an ORF allows a prediction of mRNA levels for constitutively expressed genes.
source: The geCAI score for an ORF allows a prediction of mRNA levels for constitutively expressed genes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the correlation between geCAI scores and mRNA levels.

claim: The differences in GFP mRNA levels resulted from differences in the half-lives of the mRNAs.
source: The differences in GFP mRNA levels resulted from differences in the half-lives of the mRNAs, the lower the geCAI score, the shorter the half-life.
evidence: This is supported by the sinefungin experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: The lower the geCAI score, the shorter the mRNA half-life.
source: The differences in GFP mRNA levels resulted from differences in the half-lives of the mRNAs, the lower the geCAI score, the shorter the half-life.
evidence: This is supported by the sinefungin experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: The main difference between the geCAI and other CAI statistics is that the codon weight matrix is global rather than local.
source: The main difference between the geCAI and other CAI statistics is that the codon weight matrix is global rather than local.
evidence: This is a description of the methodological innovation in geCAI.

claim: For a conventional CAI matrix one codon for each amino acid must be assigned a value of 1, other synonymous codons for each amino acid must have values ≤ 1 and>0.
source: Specifically, for a conventional CAI matrix one codon for each amino acid must be assigned a value of 1, other synonymous codons for each amino acid must have values ≤ 1 and>0.
evidence: This is a description of how conventional CAI is calculated.

claim: Conventional CAI makes the assumption that the translation efficiency of the optimal synonymous codon for each amino acid is equivalent.
source: This makes the assumption that the translation efficiency of the optimal synonymous codon for each amino acid is equivalent.
evidence: This is a statement about the assumptions underlying conventional CAI.

claim: In geCAI, at least one from the 61 codons must have the maximum value of 1 and all other codons must have values ≤ 1 and>0.
source: This local constraint (one codon for each amino acid has a value = 1) is not enforced when calculating geCAI but a single global constraint that stipulates that at least one from the 61 codons must have the maximum value of 1 and that all other codons must have values ≤ 1 and>0.
evidence: This is a description of how geCAI is calculated.

claim: In geCAI, the optimal synonymous codon for one amino acid does not necessarily have the same value as the optimal synonymous codon for any other amino acid.
source: Thus, unlike other codon weight matrices, such as CAI (Sharp et al., 1987) and tAI (dos Reis et al., 2004), the optimal synonymous codon for one amino acid does not necessarily have the same value as the optimal synonymous codon for any other amino acid.
evidence: This is a description of a key feature of geCAI that distinguishes it from other metrics.

claim: Only six codons have a geCAI value of 1 in the set of geCAI values for all amino acids.
source: In the set of geCAI values for all amino acids, only six codons have a value of 1 and there is also an unexpected variation in values between codons encoding similar amino acids.
evidence: This is an observation from the calculated geCAI values shown in Table 1.

claim: There is unexpected variation in geCAI values between codons encoding similar amino acids.
source: In the set of geCAI values for all amino acids, only six codons have a value of 1 and there is also an unexpected variation in values between codons encoding similar amino acids.
evidence: This is an observation from the calculated geCAI values shown in Table 1.

claim: All six codons for serine have geCAI values below 0.25 whereas threonine codons range from 0.75 to 1.
source: For example, all six codons for serine have geCAI values below 0.25 whereas threonine codons range from 0.75 to 1 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an observation from the calculated geCAI values shown in Figure 3B and Table 1.

claim: The vast majority of mRNAs encoding ORFs with a geCAI score of 0.35 vary between 1 and 5 mRNA molecules per cell.
source: The geCAI scores provided a prediction of a range mRNA abundance, for example the vast majority of mRNAs encoding ORFs with a geCAI score of 0.35 vary between 1 and 5 mRNA molecules per cell.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the geCAI data and its predictive power.

claim: There are determinants of the final mRNA levels that lie outside codon use.
source: This range of mRNA levels suggests that there are determinants of the final mRNA levels that lie outside codon use:
evidence: This is an inference from the variation in mRNA levels at a given geCAI score.

claim: Some variation in mRNA levels might arise from differential transcription rates of polycistronic transcription units.
source: Second, it is not known whether all the polycistronic transcription units are transcribed at the same rate, so some of the variation might arise from differential transcription rates.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible source of variation in mRNA levels.

claim: The cohort of single copy genes will include some that are developmentally regulated in one of the several other developmental forms not considered in this study.
source: Third, the cohort of single copy genes will include some that are developmentally regulated in one of the several other developmental forms not considered here.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation in the gene set used for analysis.

claim: The half-life of most mRNAs in trypanosomes is set by a translation associated process.
source: However, the predictive ability of geCAI scores for mRNA expression level is remarkable and, along with the experiments altering translation of the reporter mRNA, provides good evidence that the half-life of most mRNAs is set by a translation associated process.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the geCAI predictions and the translation blocking experiments.

claim: Many mRNAs down regulated in PCFs were expressed at levels lower than predicted by geCAI scores, which might be expected if the intrinsic geCAI expression level of these mRNAs is modulated by cis-elements in the UTRs to destabilise the mRNA.
source: Many mRNAs down regulated in PCFs (when compared to BSFs) were expressed at levels lower than predicted by geCAI scores. This might be expected if the intrinsic geCAI expression level of these mRNAs is modulated by cis-elements in the UTRs to destabilise the mRNA (Webb et al., 2005a; Clayton, 2013).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations about mRNA destabilization mechanisms.

claim: Many mRNAs upregulated in PCFs relative to BSFs were expressed at levels greater that would be predicted by the geCAI score, indicating that these mRNAs are actively stabilised in PCFs.
source: Conversely, many mRNAs upregulated in PCFs relative to BSFs were expressed at levels greater that would be predicted by the geCAI score. This indicates that these mRNAs are actively stabilised in PCFs
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that these mRNAs are more abundant than predicted by geCAI.

claim: Two comparative analyses of BSFs and PCFs by ribosome profiling showed that regulated translation was common.
source: Two comparative analyses of BSFs and PCFs by ribosome profiling showed that regulated translation was common (Vasquez et al., 2014; Jensen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vasquez et al., 2014 and Jensen et al., 2014.

claim: The evidence that reducing the frequency of translation had little effect on mRNA levels indicates that inhibition or stimulation of translation and alteration to mRNA levels are not necessarily linked.
source: Thus, could inhibition or stimulation of translation directly cause alteration to mRNA levels? The evidence here where reducing the frequency of translation had little effect on mRNA levels indicates the two are not necessarily linked.
evidence: This is an inference from the 12 bp stem loop experiment.

claim: The weak correlation between geCAI score for an ORF and the ribosome density indicates that abundant mRNAs (high geCAI score) are not necessarily translated frequently.
source: Further, the weak correlation between geCAI score for an ORF and the ribosome density indicates that abundant mRNAs (high geCAI score) are not necessarily translated frequently.
evidence: This is an inference from the analysis of ribosome profiling data.

claim: If a trans-acting factor causes ribosome slowing or stalling during translation then an effect on mRNA stability could follow.
source: However, should a trans-acting factor act in a similar manner to Fragile X mental retardation protein (Darnell et al., 2011) and cause ribosome slowing or stalling during translation then an effect on mRNA stability could follow.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism, supported by citation to Darnell et al., 2011.

claim: The differential speed of progression of a ribosome on different codons is generally held to be dependent on the supply of cognate charged tRNAs.
source: The differential speed of progression of a ribosome on different codons is generally held to be dependent on the supply of cognate charged tRNAs (Fluitt et al., 2007; Chu et al., 2011; Chu et al., 2014) and this forms the basis of the tRNA adaptation index (tAI) (dos Reis et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: In the T. brucei genome there are only 66 tRNA genes including two for selenocysteine.
source: In yeast there are >270 tRNA genes, whilst in the T. brucei genome there are only 66 tRNA genes including two for selenocysteine (Tan et al., 2002; Padilla-Mejía et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tan et al., 2002 and Padilla-Mejía et al., 2009.

claim: In yeast there are >270 tRNA genes.
source: In yeast there are >270 tRNA genes, whilst in the T. brucei genome there are only 66 tRNA genes including two for selenocysteine (Tan et al., 2002; Padilla-Mejía et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast.

claim: Codon optimality has been shown to be a major determinant of mRNA stability in yeast.
source: Codon optimality has also been shown to be a major determinant of mRNA stability in yeast ([Presnyak et al., 2015] and reviewed in [Heck and Wilusz, 2018]) and operates through the detection of slower ribosome progression by the RNA helicase DHH1 (Radhakrishnan et al., 2016) which in turn can activate mRNA decay (Coller et al., 2001; Sweet et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Presnyak et al., 2015, Heck and Wilusz, 2018, and Radhakrishnan et al., 2016.

claim: In yeast, codon optimality operates through the detection of slower ribosome progression by the RNA helicase DHH1 which in turn can activate mRNA decay.
source: Codon optimality has also been shown to be a major determinant of mRNA stability in yeast ([Presnyak et al., 2015] and reviewed in [Heck and Wilusz, 2018]) and operates through the detection of slower ribosome progression by the RNA helicase DHH1 (Radhakrishnan et al., 2016) which in turn can activate mRNA decay (Coller et al., 2001; Sweet et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Radhakrishnan et al., 2016, Coller et al., 2001, and Sweet et al., 2012.

claim: A similar process that links speed of ribosome progression to mRNA decay operates in trypanosomes.
source: The findings here provide evidence that a similar process that links speed of ribosome progression to mRNA decay operates in trypanosomes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in this study.

claim: An orthologue of DHH1 is present in trypanosomes.
source: An orthologue of DHH1 is present in trypanosomes (Schwede et al., 2008; Kramer et al., 2010) and co-precipitates with the NOT deadenylase complex (Schwede et al., 2008; Färber et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schwede et al., 2008 and Kramer et al., 2010.

claim: DHH1 in trypanosomes co-precipitates with the NOT deadenylase complex.
source: An orthologue of DHH1 is present in trypanosomes (Schwede et al., 2008; Kramer et al., 2010) and co-precipitates with the NOT deadenylase complex (Schwede et al., 2008; Färber et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schwede et al., 2008 and Färber et al., 2013.

claim: Moderate over expression of DHH1 in trypanosomes resulted in altered levels of developmentally regulated mRNAs and a slowing of growth.
source: Moderate over expression of DHH1 resulted in altered levels of developmentally regulated mRNAs and a slowing of growth (Kramer et al., 2010) but little else is known and unlike yeast, DHH1 is essential in trypanosomes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kramer et al., 2010.

claim: Unlike yeast, DHH1 is essential in trypanosomes.
source: Moderate over expression of DHH1 resulted in altered levels of developmentally regulated mRNAs and a slowing of growth (Kramer et al., 2010) but little else is known and unlike yeast, DHH1 is essential in trypanosomes.
evidence: This is a statement about the essentiality of DHH1 in trypanosomes compared to yeast.

claim: In several animals, maternal mRNAs are marked by codon use for degradation at the maternal-to-zygotic transition.
source: In several animals, maternal mRNAs are marked by codon use for degradation at the maternal-to-zygotic transition and this may reflect changes in tRNA availability or re-activation of the degradation pathway (Mishima et al., 2016; Bazzini et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mishima et al., 2016 and Bazzini et al., 2016.

claim: Changes in tRNA pools in response to external stimuli is an attractive model for regulating gene expression in developmental transitions.
source: Changes in tRNA pools in response to external stimuli is an attractive model for regulating gene expression in developmental transitions and deletion of individual tRNA genes can alter mRNA levels in yeast (Bloom-Ackermann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to Bloom-Ackermann et al., 2014.

claim: Deletion of individual tRNA genes can alter mRNA levels in yeast.
source: Changes in tRNA pools in response to external stimuli is an attractive model for regulating gene expression in developmental transitions and deletion of individual tRNA genes can alter mRNA levels in yeast (Bloom-Ackermann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bloom-Ackermann et al., 2014.

claim: The lack of selective regulation of transcription of most protein coding genes in trypanosomes means that the effect of codon use on mRNA levels is particularly apparent.
source: The lack of selective regulation of transcription of most protein coding genes in trypanosomes means that the effect of codon use on mRNA levels is particularly apparent.
evidence: This is an inference about why the codon effect is so clear in trypanosomes.

claim: If there is a common mechanism linking codon use to mRNA stability in yeast and trypanosomes, it is likely that it has a very early evolutionary origin possibly dating from the last eukaryotic common ancestor, and that it may be present in many diverse eukaryotes.
source: This is similar to the process identified in yeast and, if there is a common mechanism in yeast and trypanosomes, it is likely that it has a very early evolutionary origin possibly dating from the last eukaryotic common ancestor, and that it may be present in many diverse eukaryotes.
evidence: This is speculation about the evolutionary origin of the mechanism.
